questions.q: An operating system is best described as:
o: A user program that performs numerical calculations
A hardware component that stores the boot code
An application program used to edit documents
System-level software that acts as an intermediary between the user and the computer hardware, managing resources and their interaction
questions.e: An operating system is system-level software that performs executive functions, acting as an intermediary between a computer's user and the hardware while managing resources and their interaction.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the stated goals of an operating system?
o: To use the computer hardware in an efficient manner
To replace the CPU with software
To eliminate the need for application programs
To prevent users from executing their own programs
questions.e: Operating system goals include executing user programs and making problem-solving easier, making the system convenient to use, and using the hardware efficiently.

questions.q: A computer system can be divided into four components. Which set correctly lists them?
o: CPU, memory, disk, and network
Hardware, operating system, application programs, and users
Kernel, shell, compiler, and editor
Input, process, output, and storage
questions.e: The four components of a computer system are the hardware (basic computing resources), the operating system, the application programs, and the users.

questions.q: In the four-component view of a computer system, what is the role of the application programs?
o: They control and coordinate the use of hardware
They are the people and machines using the system
They provide the basic computing resources such as CPU and memory
They define the ways in which system resources are used to solve users' computing problems
questions.e: Application programs (such as word processors, compilers, web browsers, and database systems) define the ways in which the system resources are used to solve the users' computing problems.

questions.q: The bootstrap program that runs at power-up is typically stored where?
o: In the CPU's cache memory
In ROM or EPROM, generally known as firmware
On the hard disk in the swap area
In the interrupt vector table in RAM
questions.e: The bootstrap program is loaded at power-up or reboot and is typically stored in ROM or EPROM, generally known as firmware; it initializes the system and loads the operating system kernel.

questions.q: What is the primary function of the bootstrap program at startup?
o: To initialize all aspects of the system and load the operating system kernel to start execution
To manage virtual memory paging
To compile user programs into machine code
To schedule processes for the CPU
questions.e: The bootstrap program initializes all aspects of the system and loads the operating system kernel, then starts its execution.

questions.q: How does a device controller signal the CPU that it has finished an operation?
o: By issuing a system call
By writing directly to the CPU registers
By causing an interrupt
By halting the system clock
questions.e: Each device controller manages a particular device type and has a local buffer; it informs the CPU that it has finished its operation by causing an interrupt.

questions.q: A trap is best defined as:
o: A permanent halt of the operating system
A device that stores interrupt addresses
A software-generated interrupt caused either by an error or a user request
A hardware fault in the memory controller
questions.e: A trap is a software-generated interrupt caused either by an error or by a user request, in contrast to hardware-generated interrupts.

questions.q: An operating system is fundamentally described as being:
o: Cache driven
User driven
Compile driven
Interrupt driven
questions.e: An operating system is interrupt driven; interrupts transfer control to the appropriate interrupt service routine, generally through the interrupt vector.

questions.q: The interrupt vector contains:
o: The contents of the CPU registers
The data currently being processed by the CPU
The addresses of all the interrupt service routines
The list of ready processes
questions.e: An interrupt transfers control to the interrupt service routine through the interrupt vector, which contains the addresses of all the service routines.

questions.q: In synchronous I/O, after I/O starts, control returns to the user program:
o: Only upon I/O completion, with at most one I/O request outstanding at a time
Only after all devices finish their operations
Immediately, without waiting for I/O completion
Never; the program is terminated
questions.e: With synchronous I/O, after I/O starts control returns to the user program only upon I/O completion; at most one I/O request is outstanding at a time, so there is no simultaneous I/O processing.

questions.q: How does asynchronous I/O differ from synchronous I/O?
o: It disables all interrupts during transfer
After I/O starts, control returns to the user program without waiting for I/O completion
It permits only one outstanding I/O request
It idles the CPU until the next interrupt
questions.e: In asynchronous I/O, after I/O starts control returns to the user program without waiting for I/O completion, unlike synchronous I/O which waits.

questions.q: Direct Memory Access (DMA) is used for what purpose?
o: To store interrupt service routine addresses
To translate logical addresses to physical addresses
To let a device controller transfer blocks of data directly to main memory without CPU intervention, generating only one interrupt per block
To allow the CPU to access disk data one byte at a time
questions.e: DMA is used for high-speed devices; the device controller transfers blocks of data directly to main memory without CPU intervention, generating only one interrupt per block rather than one per byte.

questions.q: Which storage is described as the only large storage media that the CPU can access directly?
o: Main memory
Optical storage
Magnetic tape
Magnetic disk
questions.e: Main memory is the only large storage medium that the CPU can access directly; secondary storage is an extension providing large nonvolatile capacity.

questions.q: A magnetic disk surface is logically divided into:
o: Blocks, which are subdivided into words
Tracks, which are subdivided into sectors
Segments, which are subdivided into offsets
Pages, which are subdivided into frames
questions.e: A magnetic disk surface is logically divided into tracks, which are further subdivided into sectors; the disk controller determines the logical interaction between the device and the computer.

questions.q: Caching is best described as:
o: Permanently deleting unused data from memory
Encrypting information before storing it
Copying information into a faster storage system so it can be accessed more quickly
Moving all data to the slowest storage
questions.e: Caching copies information into a faster storage system; for instance, main memory can be viewed as a last cache for secondary storage.

questions.q: When requested data is found in the cache, this is called a:
o: hit
trap
fault
miss
questions.e: The cache is checked first; if the data is found it is a hit, otherwise a miss, in which case the data is read from RAM and copied to the cache for future use.

questions.q: What is multiprogramming?
o: Splitting one program across many computers
Running a single job that keeps the CPU busy at all times
Organizing jobs so that the CPU always has one to execute, switching to another job when the current one must wait
Executing only one user's programs with no switching
questions.e: Multiprogramming organizes jobs so the CPU always has one to execute; a subset of jobs is kept in memory and, when the running job must wait (for example for I/O), the OS switches to another job.

questions.q: Timesharing (multitasking) is characterized by which requirement?
o: Only one job may reside in memory at a time
The CPU switches between users' processes frequently, with a response time that should be under 1 second
The CPU never switches between processes
Response time must exceed 1 minute
questions.e: Timesharing is a logical extension of multiprogramming in which the CPU switches between processes frequently for interactive computing; a stated requirement is that response time should be less than 1 second.

questions.q: In dual-mode operation, which instructions may execute only in kernel mode?
o: Display output instructions
User input instructions
Privileged instructions
All arithmetic instructions
questions.e: Dual-mode operation distinguishes user mode from kernel mode using a hardware-provided mode bit; privileged instructions execute in kernel mode only.

questions.q: What causes the mode to change to kernel mode, and what resets it to user mode?
o: Only powering off resets the mode
A system call changes the mode to kernel; returning from the call resets it to user mode
A page fault changes it to user; an interrupt resets it to kernel
The bootstrap program toggles it on every instruction
questions.e: A system call changes the mode to kernel mode, and the return from the call resets it back to user mode, allowing the OS to protect itself and other components.

questions.q: What is the role of timers in an operating system?
o: To measure the physical temperature of the CPU
To store the addresses of interrupt routines
To prevent infinite loops or a process holding resources for indefinite periods by interrupting after a set time
To translate logical to physical addresses
questions.e: Timers are used to prevent infinite loops or a process holding resources indefinitely; the timer is set to interrupt the OS after a specific period, and when its counter reaches zero an interrupt is generated.

questions.q: How does a program differ from a process?
o: A process is stored on disk, while a program runs on the CPU
A program is active, while a process is passive
They are identical in every respect
A program is a passive entity, while a process is an active entity (a program in execution)
questions.e: A process is a program in execution and a unit of work within the system; a program is a passive entity, whereas a process is an active entity.

questions.q: A single-threaded process is characterized by having:
o: No program counter at all
One program counter specifying the location of the next instruction to execute
One program counter per thread
A separate CPU for each instruction
questions.e: A single-threaded process has one program counter specifying the location of the next instruction, executing instructions sequentially; a multi-threaded process has one program counter per thread.

questions.q: In peer-to-peer (P2P) computing, how are nodes treated?
o: Nodes cannot communicate with one another
Nodes are strictly divided into clients and servers
Only one node acts as a server for all others
All nodes are considered peers and may each act as client, server, or both
questions.e: P2P does not distinguish clients from servers; all nodes are considered peers and may each act as a client, a server, or both. Examples include Napster and Gnutella.

questions.q: What distinguishes a hard real-time system from a soft real-time system?
o: A hard real-time system is always slower than a soft one
A soft real-time system guarantees deadlines while a hard one does not
Neither type deals with time constraints
A hard real-time OS guarantees applications will meet their deadlines, while a soft real-time OS provides prioritization on a best-effort basis with no deadline guarantees
questions.e: Hard real-time systems guarantee that applications meet their deadlines (e.g. TCAS, health monitors), while soft real-time systems provide prioritization on a best-effort basis with bounded delays but no deadline guarantees.

questions.q: The description of real-time systems emphasizes that 'real-time' means:
o: Free of any time constraints
Predictable, not fast
Fast, not predictable
The same as timesharing
questions.e: Real-time means predictable, NOT fast; the goal is to cope with rigid time constraints in a predictable manner.

questions.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes protection from security?
o: Protection controls access of OS resources by processes or users; security defends the system against internal and external attacks
Protection defends against external attacks; security controls internal resource access only
Protection is hardware-only; security is unrelated to the OS
Both refer only to encrypting files
questions.e: Protection is the mechanism for controlled access of OS resources by processes or users, while security is the defense of the system against internal and external attacks.

questions.q: Which of the following is an operating-system service that assists the user?
o: Designing application logos
Manufacturing the CPU hardware
Physically printing circuit boards
Program execution (loading a program into memory and running it)
questions.e: Operating-system services for user assistance include the user interface, program execution (loading and running programs), I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communications, and error detection.

questions.q: The three types of user interface listed among OS services are:
o: Compiler, assembler, and linker
Batch, Command-Line (CLI), and Graphical User Interface (GUI)
ROM, RAM, and cache
Mouse, keyboard, and monitor
questions.e: The user interface service can take the form of Batch, Command-Line Interface (CLI), or Graphical User Interface (GUI).

questions.q: In operating systems, communication between processes may be carried out by which mechanisms?
o: Only via the interrupt vector
Shared memory, message passing, or signaling
Only through the CPU registers
Only by writing to disk files
questions.e: Processes may exchange information on the same computer or between computers over a network; this exchange is carried out by shared memory, message passing, or signaling.

questions.q: Programs typically access operating-system services through:
o: An Application Programming Interface (API) rather than directly through system calls
Direct manipulation of hardware registers
The bootstrap loader
The interrupt vector table
questions.e: System services are provided through an API; programs access OS services by system-level calls to the API rather than invoking the services directly.

questions.q: Which three are named as the most common APIs?
o: CPU API, RAM API, and Disk API
Win32 API, POSIX API, and Java API
DOS API, BIOS API, and ROM API
SQL API, HTTP API, and FTP API
questions.e: The three most common APIs are the Win32 API for Windows, the POSIX API for POSIX-based systems (UNIX, Linux, Mac OS X), and the Java API for the Java virtual machine.

questions.q: In system-call implementation, what does the system-call interface use to locate the intended call?
o: The interrupt vector's stored data values
The disk block containing the kernel
The physical address of the user program
A table indexed according to a number associated with each system call
questions.e: A number is associated with each system call, and the system-call interface maintains a table indexed according to these numbers, invoking the intended call in the kernel and returning its status and any values.

questions.q: Which is one of the three general methods used to pass parameters to the operating system?
o: Passing the parameters in registers
Broadcasting the parameters over the network
Printing the parameters to the screen
Storing the parameters in the interrupt vector
questions.e: The three general methods are passing parameters in registers, storing them in a block/table in memory and passing the block's address in a register, and pushing them onto the stack.

questions.q: Which parameter-passing method is noted as being used by Linux and Solaris?
o: Passing parameters through the interrupt vector
Encoding parameters in the program counter
Passing all parameters exclusively in registers
Storing parameters in a block or table in memory and passing the block's address in a register
questions.e: The block method, where parameters are stored in a block or table in memory and the block's address is passed in a register, is the approach taken by Linux and Solaris.

questions.q: Which is one of the listed types of system calls?
o: Process control
Cache management
Bootstrapping
Interrupt vectoring
questions.e: The types of system calls listed are process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, and communications.

questions.q: A monolithic operating system is characterized by the fact that it:
o: Strictly hides all kernel data from every procedure
Consists only of user-mode servers
Has no kernel at all
Does not enforce data hiding, though it may separate applications from the OS via user and kernel modes
questions.e: A monolithic operating system does not enforce data hiding, although it may separate applications from the OS by enforcing user mode and kernel mode limits; the typical example given is DOS.

questions.q: Which operating system is given as the typical example of a monolithic kernel?
o: UNIX
Windows XP
DOS
Solaris
questions.e: The DOS operating system is cited as the typical example of a monolithic kernel.

questions.q: In a layered operating system, each layer is given access to:
o: Only the highest layer's data structures
All layers' data structures equally
No data structures at all
Only the lower-level layer's data structures
questions.e: The layered operating system enforces a hierarchy in which each layer is provided access to only the lower-level layer's data structures, which makes debugging easier and modules flexibly replaceable.

questions.q: What is a stated advantage of the layered approach to OS structure?
o: Layering prevents any module from being replaced
Layering makes debugging easier and lets modules be flexibly replaced for updating
Layering removes the need for a kernel
Layering guarantees the fastest possible performance
questions.e: The layered approach makes debugging easier and allows modules to be flexibly replaced for updating or replacement, because each layer only depends on the layer below it.

questions.q: In the client/server kernel model, where does each server run, and what is the reliability benefit?
o: Each server runs in user mode, so if one server fails it may not crash the entire system
Each server runs in kernel mode, so a failure always crashes the system
Servers cannot run on different processors
All servers share a single process, so failures are contained
questions.e: In the client/server model each server runs separately in user mode; because the components are small and self-contained, if one server fails it may not crash the entire system, and different servers can run on different processors.

questions.q: The Solaris modular approach is described as using:
o: A strictly two-layer design with no flexibility
A design with no kernel components
An object-oriented approach where each core component is separate and loadable as needed within the kernel
A single monolithic block with no separable components
questions.e: Solaris uses an object-oriented approach in which each core component is separate, components communicate through known interfaces, and components are loadable as needed within the kernel; it is similar to layers but more flexible.

questions.q: A virtual machine provides which illusion to the operating system's processes?
o: That all processes share a single program counter
That there are multiple processes, each executing on its own processor with its own virtual memory
That there is only one process in the entire system
That the hardware has no CPU
questions.e: Virtual machines share the resources of the physical computer; the operating system creates an illusion of multiple processes, each executing on its own processor with its own virtual memory.

questions.q: What does the SYSGEN program do?
o: Performs page replacement
Schedules processes for the CPU
Compiles user application programs
Obtains information concerning the specific hardware configuration for which the system is being configured
questions.e: Operating systems are designed to run on a class of machines and must be configured for each site; the SYSGEN program obtains information about the specific hardware configuration.

questions.q: Booting a computer refers to:
o: Formatting the hard disk
Starting the computer by loading the kernel
Encrypting the file system
Shutting down all running processes
questions.e: Booting is starting a computer by loading the kernel; the bootstrap program, stored in ROM, locates the kernel, loads it into memory, and starts its execution.

questions.q: A process is defined as:
o: A program in execution
A hardware register in the CPU
The physical memory of the computer
A program stored on disk that is not running
questions.e: A process is a program in execution; it is a schedulable entity to which the CPU may be assigned by the operating system.

questions.q: According to the process concept, a process includes which of the following?
o: The interrupt vector and firmware
A program counter, a stack, and a data section
Only the disk sectors it occupies
Only the source code of the program
questions.e: A process includes the program counter, a stack, and a data section.

questions.q: How many states can a process be in, and which set is correct?
o: Compile, Link, Load, Run, and Debug
New, Running, Waiting, Ready, and Terminated
Open, Closed, Locked, Free, and Busy
Start, Stop, Pause, Resume, and Kill
questions.e: A process may be in one of the states New (being created), Running (instructions executing), Waiting (for an event), Ready (waiting to be assigned to a processor), or Terminated (finished execution).

questions.q: In the process states, what does the 'Ready' state mean?
o: The process is waiting for an I/O event to occur
The process is currently executing instructions
The process has finished execution
The process is waiting to be assigned to a processor
questions.e: In the Ready state the process is waiting to be assigned to a processor, whereas in the Running state its instructions are actually being executed.

questions.q: The Process Control Block (PCB) is:
o: The area of disk where programs are stored
A data structure used to maintain information associated with each process
A queue of I/O requests
A hardware chip that executes processes
questions.e: The PCB is a data structure used to maintain information associated with each process, such as process state, program counter, CPU scheduling information, memory-management information, accounting information, and CPU registers.

questions.q: Which item is stored in the Process Control Block?
o: The disk-scheduling algorithm
The bootstrap program
The interrupt vector table
Program counter and CPU registers
questions.e: The PCB stores the process state, program counter, CPU scheduling information, memory-management information, accounting information, I/O status information, CPU registers, the flag register, and the stack pointer.

questions.q: During a context switch, what must the system do?
o: Delete the old process permanently
Disable the CPU until the user intervenes
Save the state of the old process and load the saved state for the new process
Copy the new process to disk before running it
questions.e: When the CPU switches to another process, the system must save the state of the old process and load the saved state for the new one; this context-switch time is pure overhead.

questions.q: Context-switch time is best described as:
o: A period during which two processes run simultaneously
Overhead, because the system does no useful work while switching
The most productive time in the system
The time to compile a program
questions.e: Context-switch time is overhead: the system does no useful work while switching, and the time depends on hardware support.

questions.q: In process creation, the relationship among processes forms:
o: A tree of processes, where a parent creates children which in turn create others
A star with one central process only
A single flat list with no relationships
A circular ring of equal processes
questions.e: A parent process creates child processes, which in turn create other processes, forming a tree of processes.

questions.q: In the UNIX process-creation model, what does the fork system call do?
o: Waits for a child to exit
Creates a new process
Replaces the process's memory with a new program
Terminates the parent process
questions.e: In UNIX, the fork system call creates a new process, and the exec system call is used after a fork to replace the process's memory space with a new program.

questions.q: After a fork in UNIX, which system call replaces the process's memory space with a new program?
o: wait
fork
exec
clone
questions.e: The exec system call, used after a fork, replaces the process's memory space with a new program.

questions.q: What is cascaded termination?
o: When two processes merge into one
When a single process restarts itself repeatedly
When a terminated process's child processes are killed one after another
When a process is moved to disk
questions.e: When a process being terminated has child processes, cascaded termination usually follows, killing all the child processes one after another; however, a child created with detached status may continue to exist even after the parent terminates.

questions.q: A child process created with 'detached' status will:
o: Be converted into the parent process
Always be killed immediately with its parent
Continue to exist even after its parent is terminated
Be unable to run at all
questions.e: In contrast to cascaded termination, a child created with detached status may continue to exist even after the parent is terminated.

questions.q: A socket is defined as:
o: A type of interrupt handler
A physical connector on the motherboard
An endpoint for communication, formed by the concatenation of an IP address and a port
A block of shared memory in the kernel
questions.e: A socket is an endpoint for communication; it is the concatenation of an IP address and a port. Communication consists of a pair of sockets, e.g. 161.25.19.8:1625 refers to port 1625 on host 161.25.19.8.

questions.q: In the socket 161.25.19.8:80, what does the 80 represent?
o: The IP address of the client
The port number on the host
The size of the message in bytes
The number of connections allowed
questions.e: In a socket, the value after the colon is the port; 161.25.19.8:80 refers to port 80 (a web server port) on host 161.25.19.8.

questions.q: In a Remote Procedure Call (RPC), what is a stub?
o: The physical network cable connecting machines
The interrupt handler for network devices
A client-side proxy for the actual procedure on the server that locates the server and marshals the parameters
A block of shared memory between processes
questions.e: In RPC, stubs are the client-side proxy for the actual procedure on the server; the client-side stub locates the server and marshals the parameters, while the server-side stub unpacks them and performs the procedure.

questions.q: Remote Method Invocation (RMI) is:
o: A disk-scheduling algorithm
A Java mechanism, similar to RPC, that allows a Java program on one machine to invoke a method on a remote object
A hardware interrupt used only in UNIX
A form of shared-memory communication within one process
questions.e: RMI is a Java mechanism similar to RPCs that allows a Java program on one machine to invoke a method on a remote object, though it differs from RPC in several ways.

questions.q: In direct communication for IPC, how do processes identify each other?
o: They communicate only through a shared mailbox with an id
They identify each other by IP address only
They never need to name each other
They must name each other explicitly, e.g. send(P, message) and receive(Q, message)
questions.e: In direct communication, processes must name each other explicitly, using operations such as send(P, message) to send to process P and receive(Q, message) to receive from process Q; the link is established automatically for exactly one pair.

questions.q: In indirect communication implemented through mailboxes, communication is possible only if:
o: One process is the parent of the other
The processes name each other explicitly
The processes are on the same physical CPU
The processes share a mailbox, each of which has a unique id
questions.e: In indirect communication through mailboxes, each mailbox has a unique id and processes can communicate only if they share a mailbox; a link may be associated with many processes.

questions.q: In message-passing synchronization, a blocking send causes the sender to:
o: Receive a message instead of sending one
Discard the message if no receiver is ready
Block until the message is received
Send the message and continue immediately
questions.e: Blocking is considered synchronous: a blocking send has the sender block until the message is received, while a blocking receive blocks the receiver until a message is available.

questions.q: With zero-capacity buffering of a message queue, the sender:
o: Waits only if the link is full
Can store one message and continue
Must wait for the receiver (a rendezvous), since the queue holds 0 messages
Never waits, because the queue is infinite
questions.e: With zero capacity the queue holds 0 messages, so the sender must wait for the receiver (a rendezvous); bounded capacity makes the sender wait only when full, and unbounded capacity means the sender never waits.

questions.q: Which of the following is a stated benefit of multithreading?
o: Increased hardware cost
Responsiveness
Slower resource sharing
Loss of concurrency
questions.e: The benefits of multithreading listed are responsiveness, resource sharing, concurrency, and utilization of multiprocessor (MP) architectures.

questions.q: Which three are the primary thread libraries named for user threads?
o: TCP threads, UDP threads, and IP threads
Solaris threads, Mac threads, and IRIX threads
POSIX Pthreads, Win32 threads, and Java threads
DOS threads, BIOS threads, and ROM threads
questions.e: User-level threads are non-privileged; the three primary thread libraries are POSIX Pthreads, Win32 threads, and Java threads.

questions.q: User-level threads are described as being of which class, and kernel threads of which class?
o: User-level threads are non-privileged; kernel threads are of the privileged class
User-level threads are privileged; kernel threads are non-privileged
Both are non-privileged
Both are privileged
questions.e: User-level threads are non-privileged, while kernel threads are of the privileged class (examples of the latter include Windows, Solaris, Linux, and Mac OS X).

questions.q: Which are the three multithreading models listed?
o: Many-to-One, One-to-One, and Many-to-Many
First-fit, Best-fit, and Worst-fit
FIFO, LRU, and MFU
Direct, Indirect, and Buffered
questions.e: The three multithreading models are Many-to-One, One-to-One, and Many-to-Many.

questions.q: The Many-to-One threading model maps:
o: Each user-level thread to its own kernel thread
Many user-level threads to a single kernel thread
Many user threads to many kernel threads
One user thread to many kernel threads
questions.e: In the Many-to-One model, many user-level threads are mapped to a single kernel thread; examples include JVM threads and Solaris Green Threads.

questions.q: Which examples are given for the One-to-One threading model?
o: JVM threads and Solaris Green Threads
Napster and Gnutella
Windows, Linux, and Solaris 9 and later
IRIX and HP-UX
questions.e: In the One-to-One model each user-level thread maps to a kernel thread; examples include Windows, Linux, and Solaris 9 and later.

questions.q: The Two-level threading model is similar to Many-to-Many except that it:
o: Forbids any kernel threads
Maps all user threads to a single kernel thread
Requires exactly one user thread
Also allows a user thread to be bound to a kernel thread
questions.e: The Two-level model is similar to Many-to-Many, except that it additionally allows a user thread to be bound to a kernel thread; examples include Solaris 8 and earlier, IRIX, and HP-UX.

questions.q: What is an advantage of using a thread pool?
o: It guarantees threads never wait
It removes the upper bound on the number of threads
It eliminates the need for the kernel
It is faster to service a request with an existing thread than to create a new one each time
questions.e: With a thread pool, threads are created in kernel space and wait for assignment; it is faster to service a request using an existing thread than creating a new one every time, and the number of threads for an application is bounded to the pool size.

questions.q: In Windows threads, what is meant by the 'context' of a thread?
o: The register set, stacks, and private storage area
The entire process's memory
The kernel's interrupt vector
Only the thread id
questions.e: A Windows thread contains a thread id, a register set, separate user and kernel stacks, and a private data storage area; the register set, stacks, and private storage area are known as the context of the thread.

questions.q: How does Linux refer to threads, and through which system call are they created?
o: Linux calls them fibers and uses the fork() call
Linux calls them processes and uses exec()
Linux refers to them as tasks and creates them through the clone() system call
Linux calls them monitors and uses wait()
questions.e: Linux refers to threads as tasks rather than threads; thread creation is done through the clone() system call, which allows a child task to share the address space of the parent task.

questions.q: Java threads may be created by which two approaches?
o: Using clone() or the ThreadFiber package
Extending the Thread class or implementing the Runnable interface
Using turnstiles or adaptive mutexes
Calling fork() or exec()
questions.e: Java threads are managed by the JVM and may be created either by extending the Thread class or by implementing the Runnable interface.

questions.q: What is the difference between asynchronous and deferred thread cancellation?
o: Both terminate the thread immediately
Asynchronous cancellation lets the thread finish first; deferred cancellation is immediate
Asynchronous cancellation terminates the target thread immediately, while deferred cancellation lets the target thread periodically check whether it should be cancelled
Neither actually cancels the thread
questions.e: Asynchronous cancellation terminates the target thread immediately, whereas deferred cancellation allows the target thread to periodically check if it should be cancelled.

questions.q: In UNIX systems, signals are used to:
o: Allocate memory to a process
Notify a process that a particular event has occurred
Translate logical to physical addresses
Schedule the CPU among processes
questions.e: Signals are used in UNIX systems to notify a process that a particular event has occurred; a signal is generated by an event, delivered to a process, and then handled, with a signal handler used to process it.

questions.q: A process that continually consumes CPU bursts is called a:
o: I/O-bound job
Real-time job
Background job
CPU-bound job
questions.e: If a process continues consuming CPU bursts it is called a CPU-bound job; if it continually cycles from short CPU bursts to long I/O waits it is an I/O-bound job.

questions.q: A process that cycles from short CPU bursts to long I/O waits is called a:
o: Batch job
I/O-bound job
CPU-bound job
Kernel job
questions.e: An I/O-bound job is one that continues cycling from a short CPU burst to a long I/O wait, in contrast to a CPU-bound job that keeps consuming CPU bursts.

questions.q: CPU scheduling decisions may occur when a process switches from the running state to the waiting state, from running to ready, from waiting to ready, or when it terminates. Which pair is non-preemptive?
o: Switching from running to ready, and waiting to ready
Switching from waiting to ready, and terminating
Switching from running to waiting, and terminating
Terminating, and switching from running to ready
questions.e: Scheduling that occurs only when a process switches from running to waiting or terminates is non-preemptive; decisions when a process switches from running to ready or from waiting to ready (e.g. a higher-priority process arrives) are preemptive.

questions.q: What is the role of the dispatcher?
o: To decide the long-term admission of jobs into the system
To give control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler, involving context switching, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper program location
To translate logical addresses to physical addresses
To handle disk I/O requests
questions.e: The dispatcher module gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler; this involves switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to restart it.

questions.q: Dispatch latency is:
o: The time to complete a particular process
The time a process spends waiting in the ready queue
The number of processes completed per unit time
The time it takes for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running
questions.e: Dispatch latency is the time it takes the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running.

questions.q: Throughput as a scheduling criterion is defined as:
o: The number of processes that complete their execution per time unit
The time from request submission until the first response
The time a process waits in the ready queue
The amount of time to execute a particular process
questions.e: Throughput is the number of processes that complete their execution per time unit; turnaround time is the amount of time to execute a particular process.

questions.q: Waiting time as a scheduling criterion refers to:
o: The time until the first response is produced
The number of processes completed per unit time
The amount of time a process has been waiting in the ready queue
The time to execute a process from start to finish
questions.e: Waiting time is the amount of time a process has been waiting in the ready queue, distinct from turnaround time (total execution time) and response time (time to the first response).

questions.q: Response time as a scheduling criterion is:
o: The total time to finish a process
The number of context switches per second
The time a process spends in the ready queue overall
The amount of time from when a request is submitted until the first response is produced
questions.e: Response time is the amount of time it takes from when a request was submitted until the first response is produced (not the completion time).

questions.q: For three processes with burst times P1=24, P2=3, P3=3 scheduled by FCFS in the order P1, P2, P3, what is the average waiting time?
questions.e: Under FCFS in order P1, P2, P3, the waiting times are P1=0, P2=24, P3=27, giving an average of (0+24+27)/3 = 17.

questions.q: For the same three processes (bursts 24, 3, 3) scheduled by FCFS but in the order P2, P3, P1, the average waiting time is 3. This illustrates which effect when a short process is stuck behind a long one?
o: Thrashing
Aging
Belady's anomaly
The convoy effect
questions.e: Scheduling the short jobs first drops the average waiting time from 17 to 3; the situation where short processes wait behind a long process under FCFS is called the convoy effect.

questions.q: Shortest-Job-First (SJF) scheduling selects the process with the:
o: Earliest arrival time regardless of burst
Longest next CPU burst
Highest priority number
Shortest next CPU burst
questions.e: SJF associates with each process the length of its next CPU burst and schedules the process with the shortest such time.

questions.q: Which scheduling scheme is stated to give the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes?
o: First-Come, First-Served
Shortest-Job-First / Shortest-Remaining-Time-First
Multilevel Queue
Round Robin
questions.e: SJF (and its preemptive form SRTF) gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes.

questions.q: In Shortest-Remaining-Time-First (SRTF) scheduling, when does preemption occur?
o: When a new process arrives with a CPU burst length less than the remaining time of the currently executing process
When the current process finishes its entire burst
Only when a timer interrupt occurs
Never; SRTF is non-preemptive
questions.e: SRTF is the preemptive form of SJF: if a new process arrives with a CPU burst length less than the remaining time of the current executing process, the current process is preempted.

questions.q: For processes with arrival/burst times P1(0,7), P2(2,4), P3(4,1), P4(5,4), non-preemptive SJF gives an average waiting time of:
questions.e: Under non-preemptive SJF for these processes, the waiting times sum as (0+6+3+7)/4 = 4.

questions.q: For the same processes P1(0,7), P2(2,4), P3(4,1), P4(5,4), preemptive SJF gives an average waiting time of:
questions.e: Under preemptive SJF (SRTF) for these processes, the waiting times give (9+1+0+2)/4 = 3, lower than the non-preemptive average of 4.

questions.q: In priority scheduling, what problem can low-priority processes face, and what is the solution?
o: Starvation, solved by aging (increasing a process's priority as time progresses)
Deadlock, solved by preemption
Fragmentation, solved by coalescing
Thrashing, solved by compaction
questions.e: In priority scheduling, low-priority processes may never execute (starvation); the solution is aging, whereby the priority of a process is increased as time progresses.

questions.q: In Round Robin scheduling with n processes and time quantum q, what is the maximum time any process waits?
o: An unbounded amount of time
No more than q/n time units
No more than (n-1)q time units
Exactly nq time units
questions.e: In Round Robin, each process gets 1/n of the CPU time in chunks of at most q; no process waits more than (n-1)q time units.

questions.q: In Round Robin, what happens if the time quantum q is made very large?
o: Context-switch overhead becomes too high
The scheduling behaves like FIFO (FCFS)
Every process is preempted after one instruction
Response time becomes very good for interactivity
questions.e: If q is large, Round Robin behaves like FIFO; if q is small, response is very good and suitable for interactivity, but q must be large relative to the context-switch time or overhead becomes too high.

questions.q: In a multilevel queue with a foreground (interactive) queue and a background (batch) queue, which scheduling algorithms are assigned in the example?
o: Both queues use SJF
Both queues use priority scheduling
Foreground uses Round Robin and background uses FCFS
Foreground uses FCFS and background uses Round Robin
questions.e: In the multilevel queue example, the foreground (interactive) queue uses Round Robin and the background (batch) queue uses FCFS.

questions.q: In the multilevel-queue time-slice example, how is CPU time divided between the queues?
o: 100% to the foreground until it is empty
20% to the foreground and 80% to the background
50% to each queue
80% to the foreground in RR and 20% to the background in FCFS
questions.e: In the time-slice allotment scheme, each queue gets a certain amount of CPU time; the example gives 80% to the foreground scheduled with RR and 20% to the background scheduled with FCFS.

questions.q: What distinguishes a multilevel feedback queue from a plain multilevel queue?
o: A process can move between the various queues, which allows aging to be implemented
It uses only a single queue
Processes are permanently fixed in one queue
It has no scheduling algorithm per queue
questions.e: In a multilevel feedback queue, an array of queues is maintained and a process can move between the various queues; this movement allows aging to be implemented, unlike a fixed multilevel queue.

questions.q: In the multilevel feedback queue example with Q0 (RR, quantum 8 ms), Q1 (RR, quantum 16 ms), and Q2 (FCFS), what happens to a job that does not finish its 8 ms in Q0?
o: It jumps directly to Q2
It is moved to queue Q1 where it receives 16 additional milliseconds
It stays in Q0 and restarts its 8 ms
It is terminated immediately
questions.e: A new job enters Q0 and receives 8 ms; if it does not finish in 8 ms it is moved to Q1, where it is served and receives 16 additional milliseconds, and if it still does not complete it is moved to Q2 (FCFS).

questions.q: In symmetric multiprocessing, why is synchronization required?
o: Because only one processor may access system data structures
Because there is only a single processor
Because all processors access shared system data structures such as the ready list simultaneously
Because processors never share any data
questions.e: In symmetric multiprocessing (homogeneous processors), all processors access system data structures like the ready list simultaneously, so synchronization is required; asymmetric multiprocessing has only one processor access these structures.

questions.q: What is processor affinity?
o: The requirement that all processors run the same process
A method of translating addresses across processors
The tendency of processes to avoid the CPU entirely
Specifying that a process can run on a specific processor to avoid cache flushing on migration
questions.e: Processor affinity handles the cache flushing and repopulation required when a process migrates to a new processor by specifying that it can run on a specific processor; Solaris extends this to a group of processors, and Linux supports both hard and soft affinity.

questions.q: In multiprocessor load balancing, what is push migration?
o: Copying a process to disk
Terminating an overloaded processor
Moving processes from an overloaded processor to another one
A processor picking up a waiting process from another processor's ready list
questions.e: Push migration moves processes from an overloaded processor to another one, whereas pull migration is when an idle processor picks up a waiting process from another processor's ready list.

questions.q: Concurrent processes are those which:
o: Are known to exist at the same time and may access the same data or program sections
Belong to different users only
Execute strictly one after another with no overlap
Never share any resources
questions.e: Concurrent processes are those known to exist at the same time; they may access the same data or program sections, and such shared memory areas are called critical sections.

questions.q: A critical section is a memory area for which the operating system must guarantee that:
o: At least two processes access it together
No process ever accesses it
All processes access it simultaneously
Only one process interacts with it at a time
questions.e: Shared memory areas accessed by concurrent processes are called critical sections because the OS must guarantee that only one process interacts with them at a time.

questions.q: A race condition occurs when:
o: A process runs faster than all others
All processes finish at exactly the same time with correct results
Only one process is allowed in the critical section
Processes access shared resources in a manner that produces unpredictable results and the desired sequence cannot be achieved
questions.e: A race condition arises when processors access shared resources such that unpredictable results are witnessed and the desired output or sequence of operations cannot be achieved.

questions.q: Mutual exclusion with respect to a critical section means that:
o: Processes take turns in a fixed cyclic order regardless of need
All processes may enter the critical section together
Only one process should have access rights to the critical section at one time
No process may ever enter the critical section
questions.e: Because the critical section involves information shared between processes, only one process should have access at a time; in other words, access must be mutually exclusive.

questions.q: In a simple lock-based scheme, a process sees the lock variable is 1 and repeatedly loops checking it. This wasteful behavior is called:
o: Busy waiting
Thrashing
Rendezvous
Aging
questions.e: A process that keeps checking a lock that is set (lock = 1) enters a busy-waiting state, which wastes CPU time.

questions.q: Why can a naive lock scheme (check if lock is 0, then set it to 1) still allow two processes into the critical section?
o: The scheduler may interrupt a process after it checks the lock but before it sets it, letting another process also find the lock at 0
The critical section is too small
Busy waiting always prevents entry
The lock variable cannot store the value 1
questions.e: If a process checks the lock and finds it 0 but is interrupted before setting it, another process can also find the lock at 0 and enter; when the first resumes it sets the lock and enters too, so both are in the critical section (a race condition).

questions.q: Why must the Test-Lock-and-Set (TSL) operation be atomic?
o: So the instruction is non-interruptible, preventing another process from accessing the lock mid-operation
So it can be interrupted at any point safely
So it can run on multiple CPUs simultaneously
So it takes as long as possible to execute
questions.e: TSL must be atomic (a single non-interruptible CPU instruction): the tested variable's contents are copied to a register and a non-zero value is stored in the flag disabling other access, all in one uninterruptible instruction.

questions.q: With the busy-waiting lock scheme, a deadlock can arise in priority scheduling when:
o: Two low-priority processes finish at the same time
No process ever enters the critical section
A low-priority process L holds the critical section and a high-priority process H, which preempts L, then needs the same critical section
The high-priority process never needs the critical section
questions.e: If low-priority L enters the critical section and high-priority H becomes ready and preempts L, then H may need the critical section held by L; since H always preempts L, L can never release it, so both wait indefinitely.

questions.q: The 'progress' requirement for a solution to the critical-section problem states that:
o: Only the highest-priority process may ever enter
A process may wait forever to enter its critical section
Processes must enter in strict numerical order
If no process is in its critical section and some wish to enter, the selection of which enters next cannot be postponed indefinitely
questions.e: Progress requires that if no process is executing in its critical section and some processes wish to enter, the selection of which will enter next cannot be postponed indefinitely.

questions.q: The 'bounded waiting' requirement for the critical-section problem states that:
o: A bound must exist on the number of times other processes can enter their critical sections after a process requests entry and before it is granted
A process may enter its critical section an unlimited number of times consecutively
There is no limit on how long a process may wait
Only one process may ever request entry
questions.e: Bounded waiting requires that a bound exists on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has requested entry and before that request is granted.

questions.q: The sleep-and-wakeup mechanism was introduced to avoid which disadvantage?
o: Cache misses
Context switching
Internal fragmentation
Busy waiting
questions.e: The sleep-and-wakeup mechanism was introduced to avoid the busy-waiting disadvantage of other schemes, for example in the producer-consumer (bounded-buffer) problem.

questions.q: The producer-consumer problem is also known as the:
o: Sleeping-barber problem
Readers-writers problem
Dining-philosophers problem
Bounded-buffer problem
questions.e: The producer-consumer problem is also called the bounded-buffer problem, in which two processes share a common buffer of N entries.

questions.q: In the sleep-and-wakeup scheme, a problem arises when:
o: A wakeup call is sent to a process that has not yet gone to sleep, so the call is lost and both processes may end up asleep
The buffer size is unlimited
The producer and consumer never share a buffer
Both processes have too many free buffers
questions.e: If the consumer decides to sleep but is interrupted before doing so, the producer may add an element and send a wakeup call; since the consumer is not yet asleep the call is lost, and later the consumer sleeps forever, so both can end up asleep.

questions.q: Who introduced semaphores to overcome the lost-wakeup problem?
o: Belady
Silberschatz
Dijkstra
Turing
questions.e: Dijkstra introduced semaphores to overcome the lost-wakeup problem; there are two types: binary and counting semaphores.

questions.q: What is the difference between a binary semaphore and a counting semaphore?
o: Neither can hold the value 0
A binary semaphore counts many calls, while a counting semaphore holds only 0 or 1
Both can only hold the value 1
A binary semaphore holds only 0 or 1 (saving one call), while a counting semaphore holds 0 or a positive integer counting accumulated wakeup calls
questions.e: A binary semaphore can be only 0 or 1, so it can save only one call, whereas a counting semaphore supports a kernel-level integer that is 0 (no wakeup saved) or positive (number of wakeup calls accumulated).

questions.q: On a semaphore, what does the Down operation do?
o: Deletes the semaphore
Tests the value: if greater than 0 it decrements and proceeds; if 0 it goes to sleep
Always increments the value and continues
Doubles the value of the semaphore
questions.e: The Down operation tests the semaphore's value: if it is greater than 0 it decrements and proceeds; if it is 0 the process goes to sleep. The Up operation increments the value.

questions.q: A monitor provides a higher level of synchronization than a semaphore. Which property is guaranteed at the monitor boundary?
o: Only one process can be active within a monitor at a time (strict mutual exclusion)
Any number of processes can be active within the monitor at once
Processes outside the monitor can access its internal data directly
No process may ever enter the monitor
questions.e: A monitor is a collection of procedures, variables, and data structures grouped as a module; its data and procedures are not accessible from outside, and only one process can be active within the monitor at a time, guaranteeing strict mutual exclusion.

questions.q: Within a monitor, what does the WAIT operation on a condition variable do?
o: Terminates the monitor permanently
Causes the calling process to block and leave the monitor, allowing other processes entry
Wakes up a sleeping process
Keeps the calling process active inside the monitor
questions.e: If a monitor procedure discovers it cannot continue (e.g. the buffer is full), it executes WAIT, which causes the calling process to block and leave the monitor, allowing other previously inhibited processes to enter.

questions.q: Why must a process issuing SIGNAL inside a monitor make it the last statement (then immediately exit)?
o: To ensure the signal is never delivered
To avoid having two active processes in the critical section at once
To disable all condition variables
To keep the buffer permanently full
questions.e: SIGNAL wakes a sleeping process; if the signal originates from within the monitor it could lead to two active processes in the critical section, so the signaling process should immediately exit, making SIGNAL the last statement in the monitor.

questions.q: A stated advantage of monitors over semaphores is that:
o: The compiler, not the programmer, guarantees mutual exclusion, so it works better
Monitors eliminate the need for any mutual exclusion
Monitors require the programmer to manually manage locks
Monitors allow many processes to be active at once
questions.e: Monitors are programming sections handled specially by the compiler; because the compiler, not the programmer, guarantees mutual exclusion, it works better than manual semaphore management.

questions.q: In transaction processing, a transaction is terminated by which operations?
o: Seek or rotate
Commit (successful) or abort (failed)
Sleep or wakeup
Push or pull
questions.e: A transaction is a series of read and write operations performing a single logical function; it is terminated by a commit (transaction successful) or an abort (transaction failed), and an aborted transaction must be rolled back.

questions.q: How is stable storage characterized relative to volatile and nonvolatile storage?
o: Stable storage is the same as main memory
Stable storage is information that is never lost; it is not actually possible and is approximated via replication or RAID
Stable storage loses data every time power is cut
Stable storage does not survive system crashes
questions.e: Volatile storage (e.g. main memory, cache) does not survive crashes; nonvolatile storage (disk, tape) usually does; stable storage is information never lost, which is not actually possible and is approximated via replication or RAID to devices with independent failure modes.

questions.q: In log-based recovery, what is the rule of write-ahead logging?
o: No log is kept at all
The log is written only after the transaction commits
The log entry must reach stable storage before the operation on the data occurs
The data must be written before the log entry
questions.e: The most common technique is write-ahead logging, in which the log entry must reach stable storage before the operation on the data occurs; each log record includes the transaction name, data item name, old value, and new value.

questions.q: In the log-based recovery algorithm, if the log contains <Ti starts> but not <Ti commits>, the system performs:
o: checkpoint(Ti)
commit(Ti)
redo(Ti)
undo(Ti)
questions.e: If the log contains <Ti starts> without <Ti commits>, undo(Ti) is performed; if it contains both <Ti starts> and <Ti commits>, redo(Ti) is performed. Both undo and redo must be idempotent.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the four conditions that may lead to deadlock?
o: Seek, rotate, transfer, and commit
Aging, starvation, thrashing, and fragmentation
Compile, link, load, and execute
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait
questions.e: The four conditions that may lead to deadlock are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions.q: The 'hold and wait' condition for deadlock means that:
o: There is a circular chain of waiting processes
A process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes
Only one process can use a resource at a time
A resource can be released only voluntarily by the holding process
questions.e: Hold and wait occurs when a process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources that are held by other processes.

questions.q: The 'no preemption' condition for deadlock states that:
o: Processes wait in a circular chain
Only one process may hold a resource
A resource can be released only voluntarily by the process holding it, after that process completes its task
Resources can be forcibly taken from any process at any time
questions.e: Under no preemption, a resource can be released only voluntarily by the process holding it, after that process has completed its task; it cannot be forcibly taken away.

questions.q: Which set lists the methods for handling deadlocks?
o: Aging, compaction, and paging
Seek, scan, and look
Prevention, avoidance, and detect-and-recover
Commit, abort, and rollback
questions.e: The methods for handling deadlocks are prevention (ensure the system never enters a deadlock state), avoidance (maintain safe/unsafe usage), and detect-and-recover (allow the system to approach deadlock, then recover).

questions.q: What does the deadlock-avoidance approach do?
o: Maintains safe/unsafe usage of resources to avoid deadlocks
Ensures the system can never enter a deadlock state by design
Aborts every process at startup
Ignores deadlocks and never checks for them
questions.e: Deadlock avoidance has the system maintain safe or unsafe usage of resources to avoid deadlocks, distinct from prevention (which ensures deadlock is structurally impossible) and detect-and-recover.

questions.q: To prevent the hold-and-wait condition, one strategy is to:
o: Allow a process to request resources one at a time while holding others
Let resources be preempted arbitrarily
Require a process to get all resources it needs before it begins execution
Never allocate any resources to processes
questions.e: One strategy to prevent hold and wait is to require a process to acquire all the resources it requires before it begins execution; this is only possible for non-sharable resources and leads to low resource utilization.

questions.q: What does the Banker's Algorithm require each process to declare?
o: The maximum number of resources of each type that it may need
The priority of every other process
The exact time it will finish execution
The disk sectors it will access
questions.e: The Banker's Algorithm (a deadlock-avoidance method) requires each process to declare the maximum number of resources of each type it may need, then dynamically examines the resource-allocation state to ensure no circular-wait condition can arise.

questions.q: In the Banker's Algorithm, the resource-allocation state is defined by:
o: The number of available and allocated resources and the maximum demands of the processes
Only the total memory installed
The number of interrupts per second
Only the CPU scheduling algorithm in use
questions.e: The resource-allocation state is defined by the number of available and allocated resources together with the maximum demands of the processes.

questions.q: When recovering from deadlock by resource preemption, which consideration helps avoid process starvation?
o: Always picking the same process as the victim
Ensuring the same process is not always picked as the victim
Never rolling back any process
Aborting all processes at once
questions.e: Recovery by resource preemption involves selecting a victim with minimal cost, rolling it back to a safe state, and restarting it; avoiding process starvation requires ensuring the same process is not always chosen as the victim.

questions.q: Which are the two strategies given for recovery from deadlock by process termination?
o: Increase the priority of all processes, or decrease it
Abort all deadlocked processes, or abort one process at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated
Compact memory, or coalesce free partitions
Add more memory, or add more CPUs
questions.e: Recovery by process termination uses two strategies: abort all deadlocked processes, or abort one process at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated.

questions.q: When choosing the order in which to abort processes to recover from deadlock, which factor is considered?
o: The priority of the process and how long it has computed
The color of the process icon
The alphabetical order of process names only
The physical temperature of the CPU
questions.e: Factors for choosing which process to abort include the process's priority, how long it has computed and how much longer to completion, the resources it has used and needs, how many processes must be terminated, and whether it is interactive or batch.

questions.q: Which memory is directly accessible to the CPU?
o: Optical storage
The hard disk only
Magnetic tape
Main memory and registers
questions.e: Main memory and registers are directly accessible to the CPU; register access takes one CPU clock or less, cache sits between main memory and registers, and the hard disk is the slow backup store.

questions.q: In compile-time address binding, absolute code can be generated when:
o: The memory location where the program will run is known beforehand (a priori)
The program is moved during execution
The memory location is never known
The binding is deferred to run time
questions.e: In compile-time binding, if the memory location where the program will run is known a priori, absolute code can be generated; if the starting location later changes, the code must be re-generated.

questions.q: Execution-time address binding is required when:
o: The program's location is fixed and known before compilation
The program never uses memory
The process can be moved during its execution from one memory segment to another
There is only one process in the system
questions.e: Execution-time binding is used when a process can be moved during its execution from one memory segment to another; the code is relocatable but binding is deferred until run time, which is the method used by Windows.

questions.q: A logical address is:
o: A disk sector number
An address generated by the CPU under program control (also called a virtual address)
The address seen by the memory unit
The physical location of the interrupt vector
questions.e: A logical address is generated by the CPU under program control (also referred to as a virtual address), whereas a physical address is the address seen by the memory unit.

questions.q: Logical and physical addresses are the same under which binding scheme?
o: Compile-time binding
Load-time binding
Execution-time binding
No binding scheme
questions.e: Logical and physical addresses are the same in compile-time binding; in load-time binding the logical addresses are offset by a base address at load time, and in execution-time binding the offset is decided when the module is loaded into real memory.

questions.q: The Memory-Management Unit (MMU) is:
o: A queue of ready processes
A disk-scheduling algorithm
A hardware device that maps logical addresses to physical addresses
A software routine that compiles programs
questions.e: The MMU is a hardware device that maps logical to physical addresses; in a relocatable scheme the value in the relocation register is added to every address generated by a user process before it is sent to memory.

questions.q: In contiguous allocation, what do the base and limit registers contain?
o: The base register holds the smallest physical address and the limit register holds the range of logical addresses
The base register holds the disk address and the limit holds the file size
Both hold the CPU's program counter
Both hold interrupt addresses
questions.e: The base register contains the value of the smallest physical address, and the limit register contains the range of logical addresses; every generated address must be less than the limit register.

questions.q: In the dynamic storage-allocation problem, the first-fit strategy allocates:
o: A hole chosen at random
The largest available hole
The first hole that is big enough
The smallest hole that is big enough
questions.e: First-fit allocates the first hole that is big enough; best-fit allocates the smallest hole big enough (smallest leftover hole); worst-fit allocates the largest hole (largest leftover hole).

questions.q: The best-fit strategy allocates:
o: The smallest hole that is big enough, producing the smallest leftover hole
The first hole that is big enough
The largest hole available
Always the hole at the top of memory
questions.e: Best-fit allocates the smallest hole that is big enough (searching the entire list unless it is ordered by size), which produces the smallest leftover hole.

questions.q: The worst-fit strategy allocates:
o: The largest hole, producing the largest leftover hole
The hole nearest the base register
The smallest hole big enough
The first hole big enough
questions.e: Worst-fit allocates the largest hole (searching the entire list), which produces the largest leftover hole.

questions.q: External fragmentation refers to the situation where:
o: The CPU cannot access main memory
Memory is never allocated to any process
Total memory space exists to satisfy a request, but it is not contiguous
Allocated memory is slightly larger than requested, wasting space inside a partition
questions.e: External fragmentation is when the total memory space to satisfy a request exists but is not contiguous; internal fragmentation is when allocated memory is slightly larger than requested (wasted space internal to a partition).

questions.q: Internal fragmentation is best described as:
o: The joining of adjacent free partitions
Memory shuffled to place free space together
Free memory scattered in non-contiguous holes
Allocated memory slightly larger than requested, so the size difference is wasted inside a partition
questions.e: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated memory is slightly larger than the requested memory; the size difference is memory internal to a partition that is not used (per-process wasted memory).

questions.q: How can external fragmentation be reduced by compaction?
o: By making every partition the same fixed size
By shuffling memory contents to place all free memory together in one large block
By deleting all running processes
By writing all memory to disk permanently
questions.e: External fragmentation can be reduced by compaction, which shuffles memory contents to place all free memory together in one large block; coalescing of free partitions can also join them into bigger areas.

questions.q: In paging, logical memory is divided into blocks of the same size called:
o: Sectors
Pages or frames
Segments
Cylinders
questions.e: Paging divides logical memory into blocks of the same size called pages or frames (typically 1/2K, 4K, or 8K); the logical address space of a process is contiguous even though the physical pages allocated may not be.

questions.q: What is used to translate logical addresses to physical addresses in a paged system?
o: A Page Map Table (PMT) containing Page Table Entries (PTEs)
The interrupt vector table
A segment table with base and limit registers only
The relocation register alone
questions.e: In paged memory, a Page Map Table (PMT) is set up to translate logical to physical addresses; it contains Page Table Entries (PTEs) that relate the logical and physical address domains.

questions.q: In a paged system, the address generated by the CPU is divided into:
o: A track number and a sector number
A base register and a bound
A page number (p) and a page offset (d)
A segment number and a limit
questions.e: The CPU-generated address is divided into a page number (p), used as an index into the page table to find the base address of the page, and a page offset (d), combined with that base to form the physical address.

questions.q: In a paged system with 32-byte memory and 4-byte pages, if page 0 maps to frame 5, what is the physical base address of that page?
questions.e: The physical address of the start of the frame is frame number times page size: 5 x 4 = 20.

questions.q: In paging, per-process wasted memory (fragmentation) is limited to:
o: Half the total memory
The entire process size
A page size
One byte
questions.e: In paged memory, external fragmentation or per-process wastage of memory is limited to a page size, which is why choosing a suitable page size is important for performance.

questions.q: In segmentation, a segment is described as:
o: A single byte of memory
A logical unit such as a main program, procedure, function, stack, or array
A fixed-size block identical to a page
A disk sector
questions.e: Segmentation supports the user's view of memory: a program is a collection of segments, where a segment is a logical unit such as the main program, a procedure, function, method, object, local/global variables, common block, stack, symbol table, or arrays.

questions.q: In segmentation, a logical address consists of:
o: A track and sector pair
A two-tuple of <segment-number, offset>
A single page number
A base register value only
questions.e: In segmentation architecture, a logical address is a two-tuple <segment-number, offset>; the segment table maps this, with each entry containing a base (starting physical address) and a limit (length of the segment).

questions.q: In the segment table, what do the 'base' and 'limit' entries specify?
o: Base is the starting physical address of the segment; limit specifies the length of the segment
Base is the segment number; limit is the page size
Base is the disk block; limit is the file name
Base is the offset; limit is the frame number
questions.e: Each segment-table entry has a base, containing the starting physical address where the segment resides in memory, and a limit, specifying the length of the segment.

questions.q: The Segment-Table Length Register (STLR) is used to check that a segment number s is legal by verifying that:
o: s is greater than STLR
s is less than STLR
s equals the base register
s is a multiple of the page size
questions.e: The STLR indicates the number of segments used by a program; a segment number s is legal only if s < STLR. The Segment-Table Base Register (STBR) points to the segment table's location in memory.

questions.q: Because segments vary in length, memory allocation for segmentation is:
o: A dynamic storage-allocation problem
Identical to fixed partitioning
Always free of fragmentation
Impossible to implement
questions.e: Since segments vary in length, memory allocation for segmentation is a dynamic storage-allocation problem (first-fit, best-fit, etc.), unlike paging where all frames are the same size.

questions.q: Virtual memory is defined as:
o: The interrupt vector stored on disk
The separation of user logical memory from physical memory, so only part of a program need be in memory for execution
A region of the CPU cache
A faster type of physical RAM
questions.e: Virtual memory is the separation of user logical memory from physical memory; only part of a program needs to be in memory for execution, so the logical address space can be much larger than the physical address space.

questions.q: The two types of program locality mentioned as motivation for virtual memory are:
o: Vertical locality and horizontal locality
Static locality and dynamic locality
Temporal locality (due to code) and spatial locality (due to data)
Internal locality and external locality
questions.e: Programs exhibit temporal locality (due to code, such as subroutines, counters, and loops) and spatial locality (due to data size, such as arrays, structures, records, and lists).

questions.q: Virtual memory can be implemented via:
o: Demand paging or demand segmentation
FCFS or SSTF scheduling
First-fit or best-fit only
Compaction or coalescing
questions.e: Virtual memory can be implemented via demand paging or demand segmentation.

questions.q: With each page-table entry, a valid-invalid bit is associated. What does the 'i' (invalid) setting indicate?
o: The page is not in memory (which triggers a page fault when accessed)
The page is currently in memory
The page has been modified
The page is permanently locked
questions.e: A valid-invalid bit is associated with each page-table entry: v means in-memory and i means not-in-memory. Initially all entries are i; if the bit is i when the page is accessed, a page fault occurs.

questions.q: What is page replacement?
o: Copying every page to disk permanently
Deleting all pages of a process
Doubling the number of frames
Finding a page in memory not really in use and replacing it with a needed page from the hard disk
questions.e: When there is no free frame, page replacement finds a process page in memory not really in use and replaces it with the new page from the hard disk; the surrendered page normally goes to the Free Page List.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the modify (dirty) bit in page replacement?
o: To store the page's physical address
To reduce overhead by writing only modified pages back to disk
To indicate whether a page is in memory
To count the number of references to a page
questions.e: The modify (dirty) bit reduces the overhead of page transfers, because only modified pages need to be written to disk when replaced.

questions.q: The reference string used to evaluate page-replacement algorithms is 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. An algorithm is evaluated by:
o: Running it on this string and computing the number of page faults
Measuring the CPU temperature
Timing how long compilation takes
Counting the number of processes created
questions.e: A page-replacement algorithm is evaluated by running it on a particular reference string (here 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and computing the number of page faults, with the objective of the lowest page-fault rate.

questions.q: Belady's anomaly is the phenomenon where:
o: Increasing the number of frames results in more page faults
Increasing frames always reduces page faults
The CPU utilization drops to zero
Page faults never change with frame count
questions.e: Belady's anomaly is when more frames lead to more page faults; it is associated with the FIFO algorithm, which is described as unintelligent so its results are unpredictable.

questions.q: Which page-replacement algorithm is subject to Belady's anomaly?
o: Second-chance
LRU
LFU
FIFO
questions.e: FIFO (First-In-First-Out) is the algorithm cited as exhibiting Belady's anomaly, where more frames can produce more page faults.

questions.q: How does the LRU algorithm decide which page to replace?
o: It replaces the page that was loaded first regardless of use
It replaces the least recently used page, determined from a time stamp updated on each reference
It replaces a randomly chosen page
It replaces the page with the smallest reference count
questions.e: In LRU, every page entry has a time stamp updated each time the page is referenced; when a page must be replaced, the time stamps are examined to find the least recently used page.

questions.q: In the counting algorithms, how does the LFU algorithm choose a page to replace?
o: It replaces the first page loaded
It replaces the most recently used page
It replaces the page with the largest reference count
It replaces the page with the smallest reference count
questions.e: LFU (Least Frequently Used) replaces the page with the smallest count, while MFU (Most Frequently Used) argues that the page with the smallest count was probably just brought in and has yet to be used.

questions.q: In the second-chance (clock) algorithm, what happens when the page to be replaced has its reference bit set to 1?
o: It is written to disk and deleted
The algorithm halts
It is immediately replaced
Its reference bit is set to 0, it is left in memory, and the next page in clock order is examined
questions.e: In the second-chance (clock) algorithm, if the page to be replaced has reference bit = 1, that bit is set to 0 and the page is left in memory, and the next page in clock order (with reference bit 0) is replaced; if the page is referenced again before revisiting, it gets another chance.

questions.q: What is thrashing?
o: A situation where a process is busy swapping pages in and out due to not having enough pages
A method of compacting memory
The joining of adjacent free partitions
A disk-scheduling algorithm
questions.e: Thrashing is when a process is busy swapping pages in and out; if a process does not have enough pages, the page-fault rate is very high, leading to low CPU utilization.

questions.q: Thrashing can worsen because low CPU utilization causes the OS to:
o: Disable virtual memory entirely
Immediately terminate all processes
Reduce the page size to zero
Increase the degree of multiprogramming by adding another process, which increases thrashing further
questions.e: When thrashing lowers CPU utilization, the OS thinks it needs to increase the degree of multiprogramming and adds another process, which increases thrashing further.
