questions.q: What is the difference between global and local page replacement?
o: Neither allows page replacement
In global replacement a process can take a frame from another process; in local replacement each process selects only from its own allocated frames
Both allow a process to take any frame
In global replacement each process uses only its own frames; in local replacement it can take others' frames
questions.e: Global replacement lets a process select a replacement frame from the set of all frames (so one process can take a frame from another), whereas local replacement has each process select only from its own set of allocated frames.

questions.q: Copy-on-Write (COW) allows parent and child processes to:
o: Always duplicate all pages immediately
Never share any pages
Share pages that can never be modified
Initially share the same pages, copying a page only when one of them modifies it
questions.e: Copy-on-Write allows parent and child processes to initially share the same pages in memory; if either process modifies a shared page, that page is copied, which makes process creation more efficient since only modified pages are copied.

questions.q: Memory-mapped file I/O works by:
o: Preventing any file from being read
Storing files only on magnetic tape
Mapping a disk block to a page in memory so file I/O is treated as routine memory access
Copying the entire file into the CPU registers
questions.e: Memory-mapped file I/O maps a disk block to a page in memory so file I/O is treated as ordinary memory access; the file is initially read using demand paging, and subsequent reads/writes are treated as memory accesses, which also allows several processes to share the mapped file.

questions.q: The buddy system allocates memory using:
o: A first-fit search of all holes
A power-of-2 allocator that rounds requests up to the next highest power of 2
A time-stamp on each page
Variable-length segments with no rounding
questions.e: The buddy system allocates memory from a fixed-size segment of physically contiguous pages using a power-of-2 allocator; requests are rounded up to the next highest power of 2, and a chunk is split into two buddies of the next-lower power of 2 when a smaller allocation is needed.

questions.q: In the slab allocator, a slab is:
o: One or more physically contiguous pages, with a cache consisting of one or more slabs
A queue of ready processes
A disk sector holding one file
A single page table entry
questions.e: In the slab allocator (a kernel-space strategy), a slab is one or more physically contiguous pages; a cache consists of one or more slabs, with a single cache for each unique kernel data structure filled with objects. Benefits include no fragmentation and fast request satisfaction.

questions.q: What is prepaging (pre-paging) intended to reduce?
o: The large number of page faults that occurs at process startup
The size of the page table
The number of CPUs required
The seek time of the disk
questions.e: Prepaging reduces the large number of page faults that occurs at process startup by prepaging all or some of the pages a process will need before they are referenced; however, if prepaged pages go unused, I/O and memory are wasted.

questions.q: In paging, physical memory is divided into small fixed-sized blocks called:
o: Segments
Frames
Cylinders
Holes
questions.e: Paging retrieves processes from secondary storage into main memory using small fixed-sized blocks of physical memory called frames.

questions.q: Consider a system with 16KB main memory and a frame size of 1KB. How many frames does the physical memory contain?
questions.e: With 16KB of main memory divided into 1KB frames, there are 16KB / 1KB = 16 frames.

questions.q: In a system with 16KB memory, 1KB frames, and four processes of 4KB each, how many frames does each process occupy?
questions.e: Each 4KB process divided into 1KB pages occupies 4KB / 1KB = 4 frames.

questions.q: After two of four 4KB processes enter a waiting state and free their frames, a new 8KB process can run because:
o: The eight frames must be contiguous for it to run
The process is swapped entirely to disk
Eight non-contiguous frames become available and paging allows non-contiguous allocation
Paging requires the process to fit in a single frame
questions.e: When two 4KB processes free their frames, eight frames (2 x 4) become free; because paging allows non-contiguous allocation, the 8KB (8-page) process can use these eight non-contiguous frames.

questions.q: What is a stated advantage of paging?
o: No external fragmentation and easy swapping between equal-sized pages and frames
It uses variable-length blocks
It eliminates internal fragmentation entirely
It requires no memory-management algorithm
questions.e: Advantages of paging include being an easy-to-use memory-management method, needing no external fragmentation, and easy swapping between equal-sized pages and page frames.

questions.q: What is a stated disadvantage of paging?
o: It causes external fragmentation
It cannot use a memory-management algorithm
It may cause internal fragmentation and page tables consume additional memory
It requires variable-length segments
questions.e: Disadvantages of paging include that it may cause internal fragmentation, uses a complex memory-management algorithm, has page tables that consume additional memory, and multi-level paging may add memory-reference overhead.

questions.q: How is paging protection implemented?
o: By a base and limit register per page
By a valid/invalid (protection) bit for each page, stored in the Page Map Table
By encrypting each page separately
By storing pages on separate disks
questions.e: Paging protection uses a valid/invalid bit (a protection bit) for each page, stored in the PMT; its status can change.

questions.q: What is the key difference between segmentation and paging?
o: Segments are fixed size, whereas pages vary in length
Segments are of variable length, whereas pages are always of fixed size
Neither uses any memory division
Both use fixed-size blocks of identical size
questions.e: Segmentation works almost like paging, but the difference is that segments are of variable length whereas in paging the pages are always of fixed size.

questions.q: The Segment Map Table in segmentation contains:
o: Only the fixed page size
Free memory blocks with their size, segment number, and memory location
The interrupt vector addresses
The CPU register contents
questions.e: In segmentation, the Segment Map Table contains free memory blocks along with their size, segment number, and memory location; segments are of variable length.

questions.q: Which is a stated advantage of segmentation over paging?
o: Segmentation causes internal fragmentation
Segmentation cannot offer protection
Segment tables always use more memory than page tables
Segment tables use less memory than paging and there is no internal fragmentation
questions.e: Advantages of segmentation include offering protection within segments, achieving sharing by segments referencing multiple processes, not causing internal fragmentation, and segment tables using less memory than paging.

questions.q: Which is a stated disadvantage of segmentation?
o: It cannot achieve sharing between processes
It uses only fixed-size blocks
It always causes internal fragmentation
Loading and removing variable-length segments can create external fragmentation
questions.e: A disadvantage of segmentation is that because processes (variable-length segments) are loaded and removed from main memory, the free memory space is separated into small pieces, which may create external fragmentation; it is also a costly memory-management algorithm.

questions.q: On magnetic disks, what does the transfer rate measure?
o: The number of cylinders on the disk
The time for a sector to rotate under the head
The rate at which data flows between the drive and the computer
The time to move the disk arm to a cylinder
questions.e: The transfer rate is the rate at which data flows between the drive and the computer; positioning (random-access) time is separate and comprises seek time and rotational latency.

questions.q: Positioning time (random-access time) on a disk consists of:
o: Only the seek time
Only the rotational latency
Transfer rate plus disk bandwidth
Seek time (moving the arm to the cylinder) plus rotational latency (the sector rotating under the head)
questions.e: Positioning time (random-access time) is the time to move the disk arm to the desired cylinder (seek time) plus the time for the desired sector to rotate under the disk head (rotational latency).

questions.q: Disk drives are addressed as:
o: Two-dimensional grids of cylinders and heads only
Large one-dimensional arrays of logical blocks, where the logical block is the smallest unit of transfer
Variable-length segments
A single contiguous byte stream with no blocks
questions.e: Disk drives are addressed as large one-dimensional arrays of logical blocks, where the logical block is the smallest unit of transfer; this array is mapped sequentially onto the disk's sectors.

questions.q: In mapping logical blocks to a disk, where is sector 0 located?
o: The last sector of the innermost cylinder
A fixed location in main memory
The center of the disk platter
The first sector of the first track on the outermost cylinder
questions.e: Sector 0 is the first sector of the first track on the outermost cylinder; mapping proceeds through that track, then the rest of the tracks in that cylinder, and then through the cylinders from outermost to innermost.

questions.q: Disk bandwidth is defined as:
o: The number of tracks per cylinder
The rotational speed of the platter
The time to move the head to a cylinder
The total number of bytes transferred divided by the total time between the first request and the completion of the last transfer
questions.e: Disk bandwidth is the total number of bytes transferred, divided by the total time between the first request for service and the completion of the last transfer.

questions.q: For the request queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with the head starting at cylinder 53, FCFS scheduling produces a total head movement of:
o: 53 cylinders
640 cylinders
236 cylinders
208 cylinders
questions.e: Servicing the requests in arrival order (FCFS) from head position 53 produces a total head movement of 640 cylinders, the largest among the algorithms illustrated.

questions.q: SSTF disk scheduling selects the request with the:
o: Minimum seek time from the current head position
Earliest arrival time in the queue
Maximum seek time from the current head position
Lowest cylinder number regardless of head position
questions.e: SSTF (Shortest-Seek-Time-First) selects the request with the minimum seek time from the current head position; it is a form of SJF scheduling and may cause starvation of some requests.

questions.q: SSTF disk scheduling is noted as being a form of which CPU-scheduling algorithm, and what problem can it cause?
o: A form of FCFS that guarantees no starvation
A form of SJF scheduling that may cause starvation of some requests
A form of priority scheduling with aging
A form of Round Robin with fixed quanta
questions.e: SSTF is a form of SJF (Shortest-Job-First) scheduling; like SJF, it may cause starvation of some requests. For the example queue it gives a total head movement of 236 cylinders.

questions.q: The SCAN disk-scheduling algorithm is also known as the:
o: Buddy algorithm
Clock algorithm
Banker's algorithm
Elevator algorithm
questions.e: In SCAN, the disk arm starts at one end and moves toward the other, servicing requests until it reaches the end, where it reverses; it is sometimes called the elevator algorithm and gives 208 cylinders of head movement for the example queue.

questions.q: How does C-SCAN differ from SCAN?
o: When C-SCAN reaches one end it immediately returns to the beginning without servicing requests on the return trip, treating the cylinders as a circular list
C-SCAN never reverses direction
C-SCAN always moves in random order
C-SCAN services requests on both the outbound and return trips equally
questions.e: C-SCAN provides more uniform wait time than SCAN: the head moves from one end to the other servicing requests, then immediately returns to the beginning without servicing any requests on the return trip, treating the cylinders as a circular list that wraps around.

questions.q: How does C-LOOK differ from C-SCAN?
o: The arm only goes as far as the last request in each direction, then reverses without going all the way to the end of the disk
The arm always travels to the physical end of the disk
C-LOOK services requests on the return trip
C-LOOK moves the head randomly
questions.e: C-LOOK is a version of C-SCAN in which the arm only goes as far as the last request in each direction, then reverses immediately, without first going all the way to the end of the disk.

questions.q: According to the guidance on selecting a disk-scheduling algorithm, which perform better for systems that place a heavy load on the disk?
o: No algorithm handles heavy load
Random scheduling
SCAN and C-SCAN
FCFS only
questions.e: SSTF is common and has a natural appeal, but SCAN and C-SCAN perform better for systems that place a heavy load on the disk; either SSTF or LOOK is a reasonable default choice.

questions.q: Why should the disk-scheduling algorithm be written as a separate module of the operating system?
o: So it can never be changed once installed
So users cannot access the disk at all
So it can be replaced with a different algorithm if necessary
So it runs on the disk controller hardware only
questions.e: The disk-scheduling algorithm should be written as a separate module of the operating system, allowing it to be replaced with a different algorithm if necessary, since performance depends on the number and types of requests.
